title: Encoding Categorical Data
abstract:
Machine learning algorithms take numbers, and a great deal of real data is text.
This document covers the three techniques from the notes — Ordinal Encoding,
Label Encoding and One-Hot Encoding — built on the nominal/ordinal distinction
that determines which one is correct. It covers the dummy variable trap and why
$k-1$ columns suffice, high-cardinality strategies including one-hot on the most
frequent categories, what to do about unseen categories at prediction time, and
the modern encoders (target, frequency, binary) that the notes do not cover but
that you will meet in practice.

blocks.t: Why and What
From the notes

Convert categorical columns to numbers for ML algorithms. The three
techniques are:

blocks.cap:
Data splits into numerical and categorical; categorical splits into
 nominal and ordinal. This second split is the whole decision — it
 determines which encoder is correct, and getting it wrong actively damages the
 model.

blocks.t: Nominal vs Ordinal — the distinction that decides everything

head: Nominal
Ordinal
rows: Data has no relationship between categories
Data has a relationship — a natural order
Colour, city, blood group, payment method
HS $<$ UG $<$ PG; Low $<$ Med $<$ High; Bronze $<$ Silver $<$ Gold
Can you say one is greater than another?

blocks.t: The test to apply when you are unsure

Ask: "is category A greater than category B?" If the question is
meaningful — Gold $>$ Silver — the column is ordinal. If it is nonsense —
is Mumbai greater than Delhi? — it is nominal. A third case exists: some
columns are ordinal but with unequal spacing (Bronze/Silver/Gold tiers
are not evenly spaced in value), which integer encoding cannot express.
Ordinal Encoding and Label Encoding

blocks.cap:
The three columns you will produce. Ordinal encoding keeps one column
 and preserves the ordering; one-hot creates one column per category and
 asserts no ordering at all.

blocks.t:
From the notes: both are used on ordinal data, and they work
exactly the same

items: Ordinal Encoding works on INPUT columns.
Label Encoding works on the TARGET column.

blocks.t:
The arithmetic is identical — the distinction is purely where you apply
it, and it is reflected in the scikit-learn API: OrdinalEncoder expects a
2-D array of features, LabelEncoder expects a 1-D target.
The notes' example:

\qquad
\text{because } \text{PG} > \text{UG} > \text{HS}.
You must specify the order yourself

OrdinalEncoder does not know that PG outranks UG. Left to itself it
assigns integers in alphabetical order — HS$\to$0, PG$\to$1, UG$\to$2 — which
puts PG below UG and silently destroys the very ordering you were trying
to preserve. Always pass categories=[[...]] explicitly, listing
them from lowest to highest.
The damage from encoding nominal data ordinally

blocks.cap:
Left: integer-encoding five cities implies a numeric line. A linear
 model will fit a single coefficient to it, asserting that moving from Mumbai to
 Delhi has the same effect as moving from Pune to Kochi, and that Jaipur is four
 times Delhi. Right: one-hot places every category at equal distance from every
 other, which is the truthful representation.

blocks.t: Why the false order is not harmless
With ordinal encoding of a nominal column, a linear model fits
\hat y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{city_code}

which forces $\hat y(\text{Kochi}) - \hat y(\text{Pune}) = \hat y(\text{Pune}) - \hat y(\text{Delhi}) = \beta_1$. The model has one
parameter to describe five unrelated groups. One-hot instead fits

\hat y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \mathbb{1}[\text{Delhi}] + \beta_2 \mathbb{1}[\text{Pune}]
 + \beta_3 \mathbb{1}[\text{Kochi}] + \beta_4 \mathbb{1}[\text{Jaipur}],

giving each category its own free parameter and imposing no ordering. In
Euclidean distance, one-hot puts every pair of distinct categories at exactly
$\sqrt{2}$ apart — equidistant, which is the correct statement about nominal
data.
Trees are the partial exception

A decision tree can recover from an arbitrary integer encoding by making several
splits on the same column, so the damage is smaller than for a linear model.
It is still not free: the tree must spend depth doing it, and the splits it
finds are constrained to contiguous integer ranges rather than arbitrary
subsets.
One-Hot Encoding
From the notes
Used for Nominal Data. Each category becomes its own binary column.
The notes' worked example:
\quad$\xrightarrow{\;\;\text{OHE}\;\;}$\quad
The dummy variable trap
From the notes

If we have $n$ columns, we use $(n-1)$ to avoid multicollinearity. Even
after removing one column, all rows are still unique.

blocks.cap:
Left: the dropped column carries no information, because
 Color_Y $= 1-$Color_B$-$Color_R. Right: the
 cardinality problem — one-hot creates one column per category, so a
 500-category column creates 500 new columns.

blocks.t: Why $k$ columns break a linear model
With all $k$ dummies present and an intercept column of ones,
\mathbb{1} = d_1 + d_2 + \cdots + d_k ,

an exact linear dependence. The design matrix $X$ is rank-deficient, so
$X^{\!\top}X$ is singular and the OLS solution
$\hat\beta=(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}y$ does not exist — there are infinitely
many coefficient vectors giving identical predictions. Dropping one dummy makes
the remaining columns independent; the dropped category becomes the
reference level, absorbed into the intercept, and every other
coefficient is read as a difference relative to it.
When you should not drop a column

The trap only matters for models that invert $X^{\!\top}X$ or that need
identifiable coefficients — linear and logistic regression without
regularisation. Do not drop when:

items:
Using regularised models (Ridge/Lasso) — the penalty resolves
 the degeneracy, and dropping makes the penalty asymmetric across
 categories.

Using tree-based models — there is no matrix inversion, and
 dropping a category hides it from the splitter.

You want interpretable per-category effects rather than
 differences from an arbitrary reference.

blocks.t: High cardinality
From the notes

If a column has 500 categories then 500 new columns. The notes give the
remedy directly: OHE using the most frequent variables — keep only the
top-$k$ frequent categories, which reduces the dimensionality.

head: Strategy
How
Cost
rows: Keep the $k$ most common; bucket the rest
Replace each category by its count or proportion
Two categories with equal frequency collide
Replace by the mean target for that category
Encode the index in base 2, or hash into $m$ buckets
Learn a dense vector per category
Needs a neural network and data

blocks.t: Target encoding leaks by construction

Replacing "Mumbai" with the mean target of all Mumbai rows uses the label of
the row you are encoding. Validation scores look excellent and production
collapses. Fixes: compute the mean out-of-fold (cross-fitted), and apply
smoothing towards the global mean so a category with three rows is not trusted:
\hat{t}_c=\frac{n_c \bar y_c+m \bar y}{n_c+m},

where $n_c$ is the category count and $m$ is a smoothing strength. Use
TargetEncoder (scikit-learn $\ge1.3$), which does both.
Unseen categories

Production will show you a category that was not in the training data. Left
unhandled, OneHotEncoder raises an error and your service returns a 500.
Pass handle_unknown="ignore" — an unseen category becomes an all-zero
row, which is the sensible "none of the known categories" encoding — or
handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist" to route it into the "other"
bucket.
All transformations are fit on train only

The notes state it here as everywhere: all transformations fit on train
data only and transform both train & test. For encoders the learned parameter
is the list of categories. Refitting on test would give the columns a
different meaning in the two sets.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import (OrdinalEncoder, LabelEncoder, OneHotEncoder)
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "education": ["HS","UG","PG","PG","UG","HS","PG","UG"],
    "city":      ["Mumbai","Delhi","Pune","Kochi","Mumbai","Jaipur","Delhi","Pune"],
    "color":     ["Y","Y","B","Y","R","B","R","Y"],
    "placed":    ["no","yes","yes","yes","no","no","yes","yes"],
})

# =====================================================================
# 1. ORDINAL ENCODING -- for INPUT columns that HAVE an order
# =====================================================================
# CRITICAL: state the order yourself. Without `categories`, sklearn sorts
# alphabetically -> HS=0, PG=1, UG=2, which puts PG BELOW UG. Silent bug.
oe = OrdinalEncoder(categories=[["HS", "UG", "PG"]])       # low -> high
df["education_enc"] = oe.fit_transform(df[["education"]])
print(df[["education", "education_enc"]].drop_duplicates())
#   HS 0.0 | UG 1.0 | PG 2.0     <- PG > UG > HS, as intended

wrong = OrdinalEncoder().fit(df[["education"]])
print("alphabetical (WRONG) order:", wrong.categories_)    # ['HS','PG','UG']

# =====================================================================
# 2. LABEL ENCODING -- for the TARGET column. Same maths, different place.
# =====================================================================
le = LabelEncoder()
y = le.fit_transform(df["placed"])       # 1-D input, unlike OrdinalEncoder
print("classes:", le.classes_, "->", y) # ['no' 'yes'] -> [0 1 1 1 0 0 1 1]
print("inverse:", le.inverse_transform([0, 1]))   # back to labels for reporting

# =====================================================================
# 3. ONE-HOT ENCODING -- for NOMINAL columns
# =====================================================================
ohe = OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False, handle_unknown="ignore")
out = ohe.fit_transform(df[["color"]])
print(pd.DataFrame(out, columns=ohe.get_feature_names_out()))
#    color_B  color_R  color_Y

# =====================================================================
# 4. THE DUMMY VARIABLE TRAP, DEMONSTRATED
# =====================================================================
full = OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False).fit_transform(df[["color"]])
X_full = np.c_[np.ones(len(full)), full]            # intercept + all k dummies
print("rank:", np.linalg.matrix_rank(X_full), "of", X_full.shape[1])  # 3 of 4
print("dummies sum to the intercept:", np.allclose(full.sum(axis=1), 1))

try:
    np.linalg.inv(X_full.T @ X_full)                 # (X'X)^-1 does not exist
except np.linalg.LinAlgError as e:
    print("singular matrix:", e)

drop1 = OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False, drop="first").fit(df[["color"]])
print("k-1 columns:", drop1.get_feature_names_out())     # color_R, color_Y
print("reference (absorbed into intercept):", drop1.categories_[0][0])  # 'B'

# ROWS ARE STILL UNIQUE after dropping -- the notes' point:
print(pd.DataFrame(drop1.transform(df[["color"]])).drop_duplicates())

# =====================================================================
# 5. WHY ORDINAL ON NOMINAL DATA HURTS -- measured
# =====================================================================
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 3000
cities = np.array(["Mumbai","Delhi","Pune","Kochi","Jaipur"])
c = rng.integers(0, 5, n)
effect = np.array([100, 20, 60, 15, 90])            # NO monotone pattern
y_num = effect[c] + rng.normal(0, 8, n)
Xc = cities[c].reshape(-1, 1)

ord_X = OrdinalEncoder().fit_transform(Xc)
ohe_X = OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False).fit_transform(Xc)
print("R2 with ordinal encoding:",
      cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), ord_X, y_num, cv=5).mean().round(3))
print("R2 with one-hot  encoding:",
      cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), ohe_X, y_num, cv=5).mean().round(3))
# ~0.02 vs ~0.98 -- ordinal forces ONE slope across five unrelated groups.

# =====================================================================
# 6. HIGH CARDINALITY -- OHE on the most frequent categories
# =====================================================================
pins = rng.choice([f"P{i:04d}" for i in range(500)], 20_000)
print("naive OHE would create", len(np.unique(pins)), "columns")

# sklearn's built-in top-k: everything rarer than max_categories -> "infrequent"
top = OneHotEncoder(max_categories=20, handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist",
                    sparse_output=False).fit(pins.reshape(-1, 1))
print("reduced to", len(top.get_feature_names_out()), "columns")
print("bucketed as infrequent:", len(top.infrequent_categories_[0]))

# manual version of the same idea
s = pd.Series(pins)
keep = s.value_counts().nlargest(20).index
reduced = s.where(s.isin(keep), "other")
print("manual top-20 + other:", reduced.nunique())

# frequency encoding -- one column instead of 500
freq = s.map(s.value_counts(normalize=True))
print("frequency encoded head:", freq.head(3).round(4).tolist())

# =====================================================================
# 7. TARGET ENCODING -- powerful, and leaks if done naively
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.preprocessing import TargetEncoder
yb = (rng.random(20_000) < 0.3).astype(int)

# WRONG: uses the row's own label
naive = pd.DataFrame({"pin": pins, "y": yb}).groupby("pin")["y"].transform("mean")

# RIGHT: cross-fitted and smoothed
te = TargetEncoder(smooth="auto", cv=5)
enc = te.fit_transform(pins.reshape(-1, 1), yb)     # fit_transform is out-of-fold
print("target-encoded shape:", enc.shape)           # (20000, 1) -- ONE column

# =====================================================================
# 8. UNSEEN CATEGORIES AT PREDICTION TIME
# =====================================================================
train = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Mumbai", "Delhi", "Pune"]})
live  = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Mumbai", "Chennai"]})     # Chennai is NEW

strict = OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False).fit(train)
try:
    strict.transform(live)
except ValueError as e:
    print("crash in production:", str(e)[:60])

safe = OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False, handle_unknown="ignore").fit(train)
print(safe.transform(live))      # [[1 0 0], [0 0 0]]  <- all zeros = "unknown"

# =====================================================================
# 9. THE REAL PATTERN: everything inside one ColumnTransformer
# =====================================================================
X = df[["education", "city", "color"]]
pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("ord", OrdinalEncoder(categories=[["HS","UG","PG"]]),        ["education"]),
    ("nom", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", drop="first"), ["city", "color"]),
])
pipe = Pipeline([("pre", pre), ("clf", LogisticRegression())]).fit(X, y)
print("feature names:", pipe.named_steps["pre"].get_feature_names_out())
# One object, fitted on train, reused verbatim in production.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Encoding converts categorical columns to numbers for ML algorithms.
 Three techniques: Ordinal, Label, One-Hot.

Nominal = no relationship between categories (states of India).
 Ordinal = has a relationship (grades in school).
 This distinction decides the encoder.

Ordinal & Label Encoding work exactly the same and are both for
 ordinal data. Ordinal Encoding is for INPUT columns; Label
 Encoding is for the TARGET column.

You must state the category order explicitly — sklearn otherwise sorts
 alphabetically and silently destroys the ordering.

One-Hot Encoding is for nominal data. Every category
 becomes its own binary column and all categories become equidistant.

Dummy variable trap: with $n$ categories use $n-1$ columns to
 avoid multicollinearity; rows remain unique. Only needed for unregularised
 linear models — not for trees or regularised models.

High cardinality: 500 categories $\to$ 500 columns. Remedy:
 one-hot on the most frequent categories, plus frequency, target
 or binary encoding.
Fit on train only; the learned parameter is the category list.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Difference between Label Encoding and Ordinal Encoding?

The arithmetic is identical — categories become integers. The difference is
where you apply it: Ordinal Encoding on input features (2-D), Label Encoding on
the target (1-D). The scikit-learn API enforces exactly this.
Q. What breaks if you label-encode a nominal column such as city?

You invent an ordering that does not exist. A linear model then fits a single
coefficient across all cities, asserting that the gap from city 1 to 2 equals the
gap from 3 to 4. Trees can partially recover by making multiple splits, but they
waste depth doing so.
Q. What is the dummy variable trap?

With $k$ dummies plus an intercept, the dummies sum to the intercept column, so
$X$ is rank-deficient, $X^{\!\top}X$ is singular, and OLS has no unique solution.
Dropping one dummy fixes it; that category becomes the reference level.
Q. Should you always use drop="first"?

No. Only for unregularised linear models. For Ridge, Lasso and tree ensembles,
dropping is unnecessary and can hurt — it makes the regularisation penalty
asymmetric across categories and hides one category from the tree splitter.
Q. A column has 10{,}000 unique product IDs. What do you do?

Not one-hot. Options: keep the top-$k$ most frequent and bucket the rest as
"other"; frequency encoding; cross-fitted, smoothed target encoding; or group
by a domain hierarchy such as product category. If you have a neural network and
enough data, learn an embedding.
Q. Why does target encoding leak, and how do you fix it?

Because the encoding of a row uses that row's own label. Fix by computing the
category means out-of-fold and smoothing towards the global mean so
low-count categories are not trusted.
Q. Production sends a category the model has never seen. What happens?

With default settings, OneHotEncoder raises and the request fails. Set
handle_unknown="ignore" so the row encodes as all zeros, or
"infrequent_if_exist" to route it to the "other" bucket.
